title: Share and fuse the combinational divide/remainder datapath
motivation:
The sole prior micro_opt result is the baseline: 5.442 MHz, 12312 LUT4s,
and a 199.837 ns worst path with 156 cells through forwarding and the
execute ALU. alu.sv expresses signed and unsigned division and remainder
independently. These deep arithmetic networks are a strong candidate
for the timing bottleneck. Reducing divider duplication and per-step
decision logic should improve Fmax without increasing CoreMark cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Refactor only the combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU datapath into a shared
unsigned quotient-and-remainder network. Select signed mode for DIV/REM,
form 32-bit operand magnitudes, and run one explicit, statically unrolled
MSB-first restoring division recurrence producing both outputs together.
At each step, compute an extended trial subtraction; its borrow bit
supplies the quotient decision and selects the next partial remainder.
Use that same subtraction for the accepted remainder, so there is no
independent magnitude comparator before a second subtraction. Taper the
stage widths explicitly: after processing k dividend bits the candidate
remainder needs only k bits. Subtract the low k divisor bits with one
extra borrow bit, and OR-reduce the remaining high divisor bits in
parallel; accept the subtraction only if both indicate no underflow.
Use constant generate indices so early stages have narrow arithmetic
rather than 32 copies of a full-width subtractor. Apply quotient sign
correction from the
operand-sign XOR and remainder sign correction from the dividend sign.
Handle division by zero explicitly: quotient is 0xffffffff and remainder
is the original dividend. Preserve INT_MIN/-1 quotient INT_MIN and
remainder zero, including INT_MIN magnitude as unsigned 0x80000000.
Preserve the ALU interface, combinational latency, pipeline behavior,
and the exact RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions. The single optimization
is arithmetic factoring of the divider; higher Fmax and lower routing
congestion should improve fitness at essentially unchanged iterations
per cycle. The vendor timing result must confirm a gain above the 4.6%
acceptance threshold; a new critical path or sign/mux overhead is the
principal uncertainty.

changes.description:
Replace the real DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU expressions with one shared,
combinational magnitude divider producing quotient and remainder
through fused subtract/borrow steps. Keep all other ALU operations
and the ALTOPS branch behavior identical. Make widths and signedness
explicit and preserve all RV32M exceptional arithmetic results.

Extend the existing exact-result division/remainder tests with all
sign combinations, INT_MIN magnitudes, zero divisors, divisors larger
than dividends, powers of two and adjacent values, high-bit unsigned
operands, and deterministic random operand pairs. Check both outputs
against an integer RV32M reference with truncation toward zero; retain
the existing multiplication and ALU checks.

title: Move DIV and REM into a bounded multicycle execute unit
motivation:
The only recorded bench experiment is the baseline: 12.12 CoreMark
iterations/sec at 5.442 MHz, with a 199.837 ns, 156-cell critical path
through forwarding and u_ex/u_alu. No LESSONS.md or prior structural
attempts exist. The ALU implements signed and unsigned division and
remainder with combinational / and % operators. These imply long
dependent arithmetic networks on the common EX result path, even when
the executing instruction is a simple integer operation. Registering
a much smaller shared division recurrence should substantially raise
Fmax. CoreMark's timed list, state and matrix kernels primarily use
integer operations, loads, branches and multiplication, so the extra
cycles for division should cost much less than the frequency gain.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU hardware with one shared,
handshaked multicycle divider inside EX. Use unsigned restoring division
on operand magnitudes, with four explicitly unrolled one-bit recurrence
steps per cycle, producing all 32 quotient bits in eight work cycles.
Execute the first four-bit group on the launch edge using the captured
operand magnitudes; execute the remaining seven groups on the following
seven edges. Do not add separate initialization or sign-correction wait
cycles: sign correction can select/negate the registered unsigned result
on the completion-to-EX/MEM path. The done flag and unsigned result are
registered on the seventh edge after launch and remain stable until
acceptance. This schedule leaves room for the existing load-use or
redirect bubble while meeting the formal ten-cycle successor deadline.
Register partial remainder, quotient/dividend and divisor between work
cycles. Use a 33-bit trial subtraction and its borrow bit for each
compare/subtract decision; do not leave any real / or % operator in
the synthesized core. Compute both quotient and remainder in the same
recurrence, then select and apply the RV32M sign rules. Capture the
forwarded source operands and operation once at launch, preserve them
for RVFI, and hold the registered result until EX accepts it. Under
zero-wait buses, require every next retirement within ten cycles of
its predecessor, including load-to-divide dependencies and consecutive
divides, as required by liveness 1 10 20 in checks_si.cfg. Verify that
deadline without modifying any formal configuration.

Only a valid divide/rem instruction blocks the frontend. Hold PC and
ID/EX from launch until completion; allow older MEM/WB instructions to
drain once, and inject EX/MEM bubbles during divider work instead of
replaying its previous instruction or memory request. Existing dmem
backpressure takes priority over moving EX/MEM or launching a request.
Retain done/result until consumed, emit the completed divide into
EX/MEM exactly once, and resume the existing result forwarding and
single-channel in-order retirement. Normal integer and multiply
instructions retain their existing EX latency. Keep the exact ALTOPS
formulas for all M operations, including division/remainder, using the
same launch, wait and completion protocol as the real divider so formal
exercises its control. Maintain nret=1, decoder/trap rules, memory
handshake semantics and every evaluation invariant unchanged.

Validate arithmetic edge cases and pipeline stall interactions with
cocotb, then run the unchanged formal suite and CoreMark RVFI cosim
with both bus stalls. Evaluate the actual fitness with Gowin timing
and the marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles: even a conservative 2x Fmax
with 25% more cycles yields a 60% fitness gain, comfortably above the
4.6% acceptance threshold. This is an estimate, not a measured result;
the remaining multiplier, register-file and stall-control paths may
limit the achieved gain.

changes.description:
Add a clocked, resettable request/result divider shared by all four
division/remainder operations. Latch forwarded operands and op;
handle signed magnitudes and signs, divisor zero, INT_MIN/-1 and
remainder sign exactly. Implement eight four-bit work cycles with
four 33-bit trial-subtract restoring steps per cycle and registered
state, including the first work group on the accepted launch edge.
Register done/unsigned results seven subsequent edges after launch;
correct the selected result's sign on the path to EX/MEM without
extra wait cycles, and hold completion until acceptance. Under
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS use
the original per-operation XOR/add/sub result formulas with the
same bounded handshake timing, not unconstrained arithmetic.

Remove synthesized combinational division and modulo expressions
from the fast ALU. DIV/REM results now come exclusively from the
divider; keep the base integer operations and multiplier behavior.
Preserve all existing ALTOPS constants and arithmetic substitutions
consistently across the fast ALU and divider implementations.

Instantiate the divider and add a wait/advance handshake. Launch
once for a valid DIV/REM when an older dmem stall permits it, latch
post-forward operands for arithmetic and RVFI, and select its
registered result on completion. While waiting, clear EX/MEM to a
bubble when MEM can advance; an older dmem stall still holds the
existing EX/MEM payload. Consume each completion only when EX/MEM
accepts it, then clear transaction state so consecutive divides
and rd=x0 divides execute and retire exactly once.

Add a divider-wait input that holds fetch PC and ID/EX, including
the launch cycle, without flushing the held divide. Distinguish
frontend hold from EX/MEM bubble insertion so older instructions
drain during divider work. Maintain dmem-stall priority and the
existing load-use and redirect rules; prevent a younger load-use
condition from clearing a held division instruction.

Wire divider wait/accept control between EX and hazard logic while
preserving the exact current nret=1 ports. Keep normal EX/MEM and
MEM/WB forwarding and retirement order, with no repeated retirement
or memory side effect while EX is waiting for the divider.

Retain the complete base-ALU and multiplication correctness vectors.
Move the existing DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vectors intact to the clocked
divider suite rather than dropping arithmetic coverage; update
this suite to reflect the fast ALU's division result routing.

Exercise the divider through its real launch/result protocol with
all transferred arithmetic vectors and deterministic randomized
RV32M reference comparisons. Cover every operand sign combination,
zero divisor, signed overflow, maximum unsigned operands, quotient
truncation and remainder sign; enforce the completion bound, reset
during work, consecutive operations and result stability while
completion acceptance is delayed. Validate ALTOPS formulas in a
separate build as well as actual division arithmetic.

Add core-level divide/rem programs checking ALU/WB/load forwarding
into launch, immediate dependent arithmetic/branches/stores after
completion, back-to-back divides and rd=x0. Exercise instruction
and data ready stalls at launch and completion and an older memory
operation during divider work; assert exact retirement order and
source values, eventual progress, and no duplicate accepted memory
requests or lost instructions. Also assert a maximum ten-cycle gap
between retirements on zero-wait buses for load/divide dependencies
and consecutive divides. Keep all existing pipeline checks.

title: 64-entry tagged branch target predictor with two-bit direction counters
motivation:
The baseline always fetches PC+4 and flushes the fetched instruction whenever
EX resolves a taken branch, JAL, or JALR. IF/ID is combinational in this core,
so the cost is one lost instruction opportunity per redirect, rather than
the two bubbles of a conventional registered five-stage pipeline. CoreMark
repeatedly executes loop branches and calls; predicting their next PC can
remove many of these bubbles despite the approximately 22% bus stalls.
The measured 199.837 ns critical path runs through forwarding and the
combinational ALU. A small parallel fetch lookup should leave that dominant
path largely unchanged, allowing a cycle reduction to improve fitness.
A trace-driven cycle model using the canonical 2K, -O3, 10-iteration binary
and the exact 0xDEADBEEF xorshift bus-stall sequence reproduces the recorded
baseline bracket of 4,491,485 cycles. With this predictor it estimates
4,197,517 cycles, a 7.00% fitness gain at unchanged Fmax. A 128-entry table
estimates 4,192,535 cycles, only 0.12% faster than 64 entries, making the
smaller table the better area and timing tradeoff. These are model estimates,
not measurements of implemented predictor RTL or a new Gowin timing result.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one 64-entry direct-mapped, fully tagged branch target buffer indexed
by fetch PC[7:2], with a valid bit, PC[31:8] tag, aligned 30-bit target,
two-bit saturating direction counter, and unconditional-jump flag per entry.
A tag miss predicts PC+4. A conditional hit predicts its stored target when
the counter MSB is set; a JAL/JALR hit always predicts its stored target.
Keep prediction independent of imem_data and operand forwarding: no global
history, return stack, early branch execution, or additional pipeline stage.
Use small asynchronous-read arrays with synchronous writes; reset only the
valid bits so payload arrays remain eligible for distributed RAM inference.

Advance to the predicted next PC only when the fetched instruction is
accepted by ID: imem is ready and there is no load-use or data-memory hold
and no older recovery redirect. Carry the exact predicted next PC with the
accepted instruction through IF/ID and ID/EX. In EX compute the existing
architectural next PC, including PC+4 for an untaken branch or a suppressed
misaligned transfer. Redirect and flush only when a valid EX instruction
actually advances and this resolved next PC differs from its saved prediction.
Compare next PCs for every valid instruction so a stale BTB hit on a normal
or illegal instruction also recovers. Correct predictions preserve the
fetched successor without a flush; JAL/JALR still write their own PC+4.

Train exactly once per valid advancing EX control transfer. Allocate a
legal aligned conditional branch on either outcome, storing its computed
branch target and initializing the counter to weakly taken (10) or weakly
not taken (01); matching entries saturate toward the resolved outcome.
Train aligned legal JAL/JALR targets as unconditional, including target
changes on indirect jumps. Do not train bubbles, trapped transfers, or
instructions held by dmem backpressure; invalidate a matching stale entry
when its instruction no longer decodes as a legal aligned control transfer.
A recovery overrides imem or load-use stalls once EX can advance, while a
dmem hold defers both recovery and training until that instruction advances.
Hold saved prediction metadata with the instruction throughout stalls.

Preserve the existing decoder, ALU, memory semantics, NRET=1 interface,
monotonic retirement order, and resolved RVFI pc_wdata. Verify prediction
recovery under overlapping imem/dmem stalls and load dependencies, then run
the unchanged formal, cosim, canonical CoreMark CRC/marker checks, and Gowin
fitness evaluation. The claim is fewer CoreMark cycles at similar median
Fmax; no correctness or evaluation contract is relaxed. The modeled cycle
gain can tolerate approximately a 2.2% Fmax reduction while still clearing
the required 4.6% improvement over the champion. Keep the table small and
avoid adding predictor logic to ALU operands, forwarding, or memory outputs.

changes.description:
Add the 64-entry tagged target buffer and two-bit direction counters,
asynchronous fetch lookup, single EX update port, valid-bit reset,
aligned-target allocation, saturating training, and stale-entry removal.

Add predicted_next_pc to if_id_t and id_ex_t; keep architectural pc_next
and all retirement payloads independent of speculation.

Wire the predictor lookup to the fetch PC and EX resolution feedback to
its update port. Gate resolution and training on valid EX advancement,
using the existing data-memory hold signal, without changing top-level IO.

Select the predicted next PC on an accepted fetch, expose it in the
fetch bundle, and retain recovery-over-stall priority. Hold PC when the
fetch is not consumed and suppress wrong-path payloads only on recovery.

Latch predicted_next_pc with the instruction and preserve it during
holds; clear it with invalid bubbles and recovery flushes.

Interpret redirect as an EX prediction mismatch, preserving existing
load-use and bus-stall behavior. Flush only for recovery and defer it
during a data-memory hold so correctly predicted successors are retained.

Test cold misses, counter saturation and loop exits, full-tag collisions,
reset validity, unconditional and changing JALR targets, and no duplicate
updates while held. Exercise core recovery for both prediction directions,
stale non-control hits, misaligned transfers, load-dependent branches,
and overlapping bus stalls; check single-channel RVFI order and next PCs.
